extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, students and scholars of philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Transcribed public lectures (Hibbert Lectures) by William James presenting and evaluating competing philosophical types (empiricism/rationalism, monism/pluralism, theism/pantheism) and offering methodological and stylistic remarks on doing philosophy. The text is aimed at making complex metaphysical distinctions intelligible to a general but educated audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned philosophical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “A philosophy, as James Ferrier used to tell us, must indeed be true, but that is the least of its requirements. One may be true without being a philosopher, true by guesswork or by revelation. What distinguishes a philosopher's truth is that it is reasoned. Argument, not supposition, must have put it in his possession.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical claims should be supported by explicit premises, argumentation, and engagement with objections; the professional philosopher values the premises, the sense in which a belief is taken, the objections it eludes, and the technical apparatus that goes with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and accessibility (avoid over-technicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The abuse of technicality is seen in the infrequency with which, in philosophical literature, metaphysical questions are discussed directly... Simplicity of statement is deemed synonymous with hollowness and shallowness... To teach philosophy so that the pupils' interest in technique exceeds that in results is surely a vicious aberration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear, simple expression over obscurantist or needlessly technical language; make philosophical results intelligible and avoid treating technique as an end rather than a means. Popular or literary expression should not be automatically discredited as 'unscientific.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as expression of personal vision
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let me repeat once more that a man's vision is the great fact about him. ... A philosophy is the expression of a man's intimate character, and all definitions of the universe are but the deliberately adopted reactions of human characters upon it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that philosophical systems often reflect temperamental or personal perspectives; writers should be transparent about the analogies and parts of experience that shaped their view and admit the role of personal vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empiricism vs. Rationalism (methodological classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Empiricism means the habit of explaining wholes by parts, and rationalism means the habit of explaining parts by wholes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction as a primary axis for classifying and evaluating philosophical approaches: empiricist works ground wholes in experienced parts; rationalist works deduce parts from assumed wholes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monism vs. Pluralism (ontological classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pluralism versus Monism: The 'each-form' and the 'all-form' of representing the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metaphysical positions by whether they present the world as essentially one unified all (monism) or as composed of many coexisting particulars (pluralism), and consider the paradoxes and consequences each view introduces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theism vs. Pantheism (intimacy vs. foreignness in spiritualism)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dualistic theism ... leaves Man an outsider, ... Pantheism identifies Man with God, ... Pantheistic idealism ... attains this higher reach of intimacy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing religious or spiritual philosophies, consider the degree of 'intimacy' they ascribe between humans and the divine: theistic (dualistic) views preserve separation, pantheistic (monistic) views emphasize fusion and mutual implication, with moral and existential consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding philosophy in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “The only material we have at our disposal for making a picture of the whole world is supplied by the various portions of that world of which we have already had experience. We can invent no new forms of conception, applicable to the whole exclusively, and not suggested originally by the parts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical theorizing should be constrained and informed by experiential data and by the particular features of the world that have been encountered; avoid inventing wholesale conceptual forms detached from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive appeal to authority; resist shopworn citation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Almost always [metaphysical questions] are handled as if through a heavy woolen curtain, the veil of previous philosophers' opinions. Alternatives are wrapped in proper names, as if it were indecent for a truth to go naked.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hide arguments behind canonical names or rely primarily on quotation from authorities; present ideas plainly and argue them on their own merits rather than by association with famous predecessors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of philosophy: divest the world of strangeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Hegel: “'The aim of knowledge,' says Hegel, 'is to divest the objective world of its strangeness, and to make us more at home in it.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophical work by its success in making experience intelligible and in helping readers feel 'at home' in the world; usefulness includes psychological and existential appropriation of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave other interests open (avoid totalizing systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: “No matter what doors it closes, it must leave other doors open for the interests which it neglects. ... The most a philosophy can hope for is not to lock out any interest forever.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of philosophical systems that claim to close off other legitimate concerns; good philosophy acknowledges its partiality and preserves space for alternative interests and approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize results and human relevance over professional in-group technique
rubrics_metrics.description: “With this exclusion of the open air all true perspective gets lost... To teach philosophy so that the pupils' interest in technique exceeds that in results is surely a vicious aberration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works by their substantive contributions and relevance to human concerns rather than by their conformity to narrowly professionalized technical standards or in-group scholastic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public orientation and intelligibility for lecture-audience
rubrics_metrics.description: “As these lectures are meant to be public, and so few, I have assumed all very special problems to be excluded, and some topic of general interest required.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing lectures or essays intended for a public audience, simplify scope, exclude overly specialized problems, and aim for intelligibility in a single hearing; favor general interest and clarity.
